summary: Provides models and manageable objects for printing environments, covering both physical and logical entities within a printing device. It obsoletes RFC 1759.

eli5.summary: This is the dashboard for a printer, showing things like paper trays and ink levels that tools can read.

questions: how to monitor printers with snmp
how to monitor printer toner with snmp
subtitle: A standard set of SNMP objects for asking a printer what it is, what state it is in, and what is wrong with it.

tldr.problem: Management applications need a common way to learn about a printer's configuration, current status and problems such as an empty toner cartridge or a paper jam, whatever the vendor.
tldr.mechanism: The Printer MIB models a printer as 13 types of sub-units (inputs, outputs, markers, media paths, interpreters, console, alerts and so on) and defines SNMP objects for describing each one, reporting its status and listing active alerts.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3805 obsoletes RFC 1759 while staying backward compatible with it, and adds new objects, a new alert notification and a companion IANA-maintained MIB of enumerations.

today: RFC 3805 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1759, and it works alongside the Finisher MIB in RFC 3806.

sections.title: Why a Printer MIB
sections.content:
Managing a printed document covers a lot: choosing a printer, queuing, scheduling and notifying the user. RFC 3805 covers only the management of the printer. It defines models and manageable objects for printing environments, for both physical and logical entities within a printing device.

The objects live in a Management Information Base (MIB) and are normally read and written with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The module is written in SMIv2, and the RFC uses the requirement words MUST, SHOULD and MAY in the sense of RFC 2119.

The RFC sorts printer information into three categories. Descriptions are mostly static facts about configuration and capability. Status is the current operating state of the printer and its parts. Alerts are reportable events, which are changes of state that matter to a management application.
sections.eli5: It is like a car dashboard for printers. Some things tell you what kind of car it is, some show what is happening now, and some light up when something goes wrong.

sections.title: The Printer Model
sections.content:
The model has three parts: the flow of a print file into an interpreter and onto the marker, the flow of media through the marker, and the auxiliary sub-units that control and support those two flows. Print data arrives through a physical connection running some transport protocol stack, appears on a channel, and goes to an interpreter that turns it into a form suitable for marking on the media.

Media sits in input sub-units, travels along a media path to a marker, and then goes to an output sub-unit, optionally with finishing. All the software sub-units run on a system controller that represents the processor, memory and storage of the printer.

All sub-units other than Alerts report only state information, either a description or a status. The Alerts sub-unit reports events. The RFC notes that sub-units do not necessarily match any physically identifiable mechanism: an interpreter for a page description language is a sub-unit too.
sections.eli5: Think of a printer as an assembly line: the job comes in, gets turned into a picture, paper is picked from a tray, gets inked, and lands in an output tray.

sections.title: The 13 Sub-Units
sections.content:
A printer is composed of 13 types of sub-units, called groups, and each gets its own part of the MIB.

  • General printer: exactly one per printer. It carries overall status, allows a reset, and covers the covers and localization.
  • Inputs and Media: one or more feeding mechanisms, and a description of the media currently in each. There is one input sub-unit per distinctly selectable input address.
  • Outputs: one or more mechanisms receiving marked media, addressed either as mailboxes or as slots for collated copies.
  • Finishers: stapling, punching, binding, inserting or folding, described in the companion Finisher MIB (RFC 3806).
  • Markers: the generalized marking process, including supplies such as toner or fuser oil. A printer may have more than one marker.
  • Media paths: the mechanisms that move media between inputs, markers, outputs and finishers, for example simplex and duplex paths.
  • System controller: represented by the Host Resources MIB (RFC 2790).
  • Interfaces: represented by the Interfaces Group of MIB-II (RFC 1213, RFC 2863).
  • Print job delivery channels: independent sources of print data, each of which can be enabled or disabled.
  • Interpreters: both page description language interpreters and control language interpreters.
  • Console: at most one operator console, which can be read and modified remotely.
  • Alerts: detects reportable events and records them in the alert table.
sections.eli5: The printer is split into thirteen kinds of parts, such as trays, ink and the screen. Each kind has its own page of questions you can ask.

sections.title: Reporting Status
sections.content:
Status is reported at three levels: the printer as a whole is reported in the Host Resources MIB, each sub-unit reports in the main table of its own group, and alert codes appear in the alert table. The RFC names a handful of interesting states, such as Idle, Active, Busy, Standby, Unavailable, and Critical or Non Critical Alert Active, and shows how they map onto hrDeviceStatus, hrPrinterStatus and hrPrinterDetectedErrorState.

The mapping is lossy. If both critical and non-critical alerts are pending, Critical Alert Active prevails. A printer in Standby appears as running(2) with printer status other(1), which does not uniquely identify that state.

For sub-units, the status column holds an integer, the sum of five parts: availability (0 to 6 in the table), non-critical alerts (8), critical alerts (16), off-line (32) and transitioning to the intended state (64). The RFC's example is an input tray that jammed on the next to last page, which may show a status of 27: unavailable because broken (3), plus a critical state (16) and a non-critical state (8).
sections.eli5: Each part reports its mood as one number made by adding up small scores. Add the scores for broken, a big problem and a small problem, and you get a single number that says it all.

sections.title: Alerts and the Alert Table
sections.content:
The Alert Group is a single table holding every currently active alert. Each entry records the severity, the group and entry where the state change happened, a more detailed location, an alert code, a description and the level of training needed to service it. One table is used because one sub-unit can cause several alerts at once, such as paper jams in several places in a media path.

Alerts are critical when the printer is stopped until the condition is fixed (out of paper, toner empty, output bin full) and non-critical otherwise (input media low, toner low). The alert sub-unit sends a trap only for critical alerts, with the exception of the alertRemovalofBinaryChangeEntry case. Whether or not a trap is sent, the management application is expected to poll the printer regularly and read the table.

The table is sparse and holds only active alerts. Binary change events come in pairs: the leading edge creates an entry and the trailing edge removes it. Unary change events, such as changing the paper from letter to legal, have no return, so there is no obvious time to remove them. When the table is full, the agent should delete a non-critical unary alert first, then a non-critical binary alert, and a critical alert only as a last resort, suggesting the oldest each time. A critical alert that was dropped should be re-added when space allows if the condition still exists. Because the alert index only increases, gaps in it tell a manager it may have missed something.
sections.eli5: The printer keeps a to-do list of problems that are happening right now. When a problem is fixed it crosses itself off. If the list gets too full, it throws away the smallest worries first.

sections.title: Read-Write Objects and Enumerations
sections.content:
Some objects describe resources a printer may be unable to sense, such as the size of paper in a tray. These are given read-write access so a console or management application can tell the printer what is installed. The printer then believes what it is told and acts on it, so the objects are not a place for sticky notes. A printer is free to allow writes only when it cannot sense the value itself. Whether values survive power cycles is implementation specific, except that prtMarkerLifeCount must persist for the lifetime of the printer if anything does.

Many sets of values are defined as textual conventions. Type 1 conventions are fully defined in the Printer MIB, so adding a value needs a new Printer MIB. Type 2 conventions live in the companion IANA Printer MIB (section 5 of the RFC), and additions need an RFC or a Designated Expert Review as described in RFC 2434. For integer objects the MIB defines special values other(-1), unknown(-2) and partial(-3), where partial means some supply or capacity remains but the amount is not known.
sections.eli5: If a printer cannot tell what size paper you put in, you can write it on a sticky label for it, and the printer will trust the label. The list of possible labels is kept in a shared notebook that only a few people may add to.

sections.title: Localization and Other MIBs
sections.content:
A Printer MIB implementation must also support parts of other MIBs. The system group and the Interfaces Group of MIB-II must be implemented, the latter for every print information interface including non-network ones. The storage and device groups of the Host Resources MIB must be implemented to represent the system controller.

The general printer sub-unit has a Localization table that identifies the natural language, country and character set of certain strings. Localization applies only to description strings and console text. The agent SHALL return all other strings in character sets where code positions 0 to 127 are US-ASCII, and SHOULD return them in UTF-8 (RFC 3629) to follow the IETF policy in RFC 2277. Control codes 0 to 31 and 127 SHALL NOT be used unless an object's description requires it. The RFC's Internationalization Considerations section simply points to this discussion.
sections.eli5: A printer's screen can speak different languages, but behind the scenes everything else should be written in a plain alphabet that all tools can read.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 1759
sections.content:
RFC 3805 supersedes RFC 1759, but a compliant RFC 1759 implementation is also compliant with this document. The new objects are optional, so the update is backward compatible.

The changes include new objects for the printer name and serial number, startup and banner sheets (the Auxiliary Sheet Group), the Input Switching Group, and counters of critical and of all alert events. Most enumerations became textual conventions, with 28 added. The alert codes were updated to include generic codes, and an optional unary event alertRemovalOfBinaryChangeEntry(1801) was added. The error state bit coverOpen was renamed doorOpen to match RFC 2790, and the alert codes doorOpen(501) and doorClosed(502) were deprecated in favor of coverOpened(3) and coverClosed(4). All objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write now also have a MIN-ACCESS of read-only.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the printer question list. Old printers that answered the first list still pass, and the new questions are optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many objects are read-write or read-create, and they can be sensitive in some environments. The RFC lists them with the harm of misuse, for example possible data loss for prtGeneralReset and possible severe inconvenience for prtConsoleDisable or prtGeneralPrinterName.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may read or change these objects. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features with authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects. Conformance rules also let vendors implement read-write objects as read-only.
sections.eli5: Some of the printer's switches could be flipped by the wrong person to cause trouble. The RFC says to use the safer, locked version of SNMP so only the right people can touch them.
